questions.q: Discuss the causes of the Revolt of 1857.
answer: The Revolt of 1857 was the result of long-building discontent with British rule, sparked by a military grievance.

answer.text: British expansion through annexations, especially the Doctrine of Lapse and the seizure of Awadh in 1856, angered rulers and nobles who lost their thrones and pensions.
Heavy land revenue ruined peasants, while cheap British imports destroyed the livelihood of artisans and craftsmen, spreading distress in town and country.
Many Indians feared that the British aimed to interfere with their religion and convert them to Christianity, and resented certain social reforms as attacks on custom.
The introduction of the new Enfield rifle, whose cartridges were rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat, offended both Hindu and Muslim sepoys and provided the spark at Meerut in May 1857.

answer: Thus political, economic, social and military grievances together produced the great revolt.

questions.q: How did the Revolt of 1857 spread, and why did it fail?

answer.text: began among the sepoys and spread rapidly across north and central India, uniting many groups against British rule.

list: It spread from Meerut to Delhi, where the rebels proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar their leader
Sepoys, peasants, artisans and dispossessed rulers joined across many towns and regions
It lacked unified leadership, a common plan and modern weapons against the well-organised British forces
Many rulers and regions stayed loyal to the British or aloof, and the rebellion was crushed with great force by 1858

questions.q: How is the Revolt of 1857 remembered, and why is it seen as a turning point?

answer.text: is remembered as a great, if failed, challenge to British rule, and it marked a turning point in Indian history.

list: To later nationalists it became the 'First War of Independence', a symbol of resistance and sacrifice
Its heroes, like Rani Lakshmibai, were celebrated in stories, pictures and songs

answer.lead: It changed how India was ruled.

list: It ended the rule of the East India Company and brought India directly under the British Crown
It made the British rule more cautiously, reshaping the army and their policies towards princes and religion
